lesson.title: The Clues That Reveal Relationships: Shared Derived Characters
lesson.summary: Shared derived characters, or synapomorphies, are traits that arose in a common ancestor and are shared by all of its descendants, and they are the specific type of evidence cladistics uses to determine which species are most closely related.
lesson.body:
Shared derived characters, which biologists also call synapomorphies, are the specific kind of evidence that makes cladistics work, and understanding exactly what qualifies as one is essential to using the method correctly. A character is "derived" if it is a relatively new trait, one that evolved partway through the history of a group rather than being present from the very start. A derived character becomes "shared" and useful for classification when it is found in two or more lineages because they inherited it from the same common ancestor in which it first evolved, meaning every descendant of that ancestor carries the trait (or, occasionally, a modified or lost version of it) while lineages outside that ancestor's descendants do not.

It helps enormously to place shared derived characters against two things they are commonly confused with, because the whole logic of cladistics depends on telling all three apart. The first contrast is with shared primitive characters, or symplesiomorphies, traits that are old and shared simply because they were already present in a more distant common ancestor and never changed. In the vertebrate example from the previous chapter, having a backbone is shared by lampreys, fish, frogs, lizards, and mammals alike, which makes it useful for recognizing that all of them belong to the larger group Vertebrata, but useless for figuring out which of them are more closely related to each other within that group, since a symplesiomorphy does not track any more recent split. Only a derived trait, one that is new relative to the specific comparison being made, carries information about relationships within the group being examined. This is also why the same trait can be a symplesiomorphy at one level of comparison and a synapomorphy at another, having a backbone is uninformative when comparing vertebrates to each other, but it becomes a genuinely useful shared derived character if the comparison is broadened to include invertebrates as an outgroup, since it would then mark all vertebrates as a clade distinct from animals lacking a backbone.

The second, and arguably more important, contrast is with analogous traits produced by convergent evolution, which resemble each other in form or function but did not come from a shared ancestor that had the trait. This is where comparative anatomy earns its keep as a source of evidence, because distinguishing a true synapomorphy from a convergent look-alike often comes down to careful anatomical detail. The streamlined body shape shared by sharks, dolphins, and ichthyosaurs looks similar at a glance, but comparative anatomy reveals it is built from very different underlying skeletal and muscular arrangements in each lineage, consistent with three separate, independent origins rather than one shared ancestral trait, exactly what you would predict from what you already learned about convergent evolution. A genuine synapomorphy, by contrast, typically shows detailed structural correspondence traceable to a single origin. The amniotic egg is a strong real example: reptiles, birds, and mammals all show the same underlying set of embryonic membranes, evidence that this reproductive innovation evolved once in a common ancestor and was inherited, sometimes in modified form, by every one of its descendants, which is exactly why amniotes are recognized as a legitimate clade.

Feathers provide another well documented and increasingly well studied case. Feathers were once thought to be a defining trait unique to birds, but the discovery of numerous fossil theropod dinosaurs preserving feather impressions or feather-like filamentous structures has shown that feathers, or at least their evolutionary precursors, arose earlier, within the theropod dinosaur lineage that birds themselves belong to. Under cladistic reasoning, this means feathers function as a shared derived character uniting birds with certain theropod dinosaur relatives, direct anatomical evidence supporting the now well established conclusion that birds are, cladistically, a lineage of surviving theropod dinosaurs, not a separate group that merely resembles them.

Pulling this together, identifying shared derived characters correctly is the single most important skill underlying cladistics and, by extension, the construction of every cladogram you studied in the previous chapter. Get the identification wrong, mistake a symplesiomorphy or a convergent trait for a genuine synapomorphy, and the resulting branching pattern will misrepresent the real history of common descent. Get it right, and the resulting clades faithfully capture the pattern of ancestry and splitting that speciation, whether allopatric, sympatric, or unfolding as part of an adaptive radiation, actually produced.
